newsitem.title: UK: Ireland's Spring cautious on hopes for IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Spring cautious on hopes for IRA truce.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said strenuous efforts were being made to achieve a new IRA guerrilla truce but stressed he had no information about whether such a ceasefire was imminent.

"We are all working very hard to see if we can bring about a cessation of violence," Spring said late on Wednesday after three hours of talks with Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, designed to give new impetus to a drive for peace in British-ruled Northern Ireland.
"The objective of the exercise is to bring about peace on this island and to ensure that we can have all of the parties negotiating at the table," Spring told reporters in Belfast.

The talks were held amid uncertainty about the two-year peace effort. Concern has been expressed by Protestant "Loyalist" groups that multi-party talks might soon collapse because of problems over the key issue of arms "decommissioning".
Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, says that it is pursuing a peace strategy and wants to get into all-party talks, but Britain and Ireland insist on an IRA guerrilla truce first.
The IRA broke a 17-month ceasefire in February with a series of bomb attacks on the British mainland.

Asked whether he had a basis for any optimism about an early ceasefire by the guerrillas who are fighting to end British rule over Northern Ireland, Spring replied: "No, I have stated consistently I have no information one way or the other."
In a joint communique, the two ministers identified an "unequivocal restoration of the IRA ceasefire" as the key element that would act as a passport to talks for Sinn Fein.
Mayhew sidestepped Sinn Fein complaints of British tardiness in replying to unspecified proposals which the republicans say might win a truce.
When questioned about Sinn Fein's claims, Mayhew said that Britain stood by its demand for an IRA truce and a demonstration by the republican guerrillas of a commitment to peace.
"We are not prepared to move away from that," he said. Mayhew described the talks with Spring as positive and constructive.

The ministers' joint statement supported a proposal by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, who is chairing multi-party talks which exclude Sinn Fein, that guerrilla forces should disarm in parallel with political talks.
They urged rival parties to end squabbles over guerrilla disarming that have held up progress in the talks, and press ahead with full negotiations on ending sectarian strife.
He dismissed predictions by Loyalists groups that the Mitchell talks were on the verge of collapse but sounded a warning note about their momentum.
"I think that there is a danger that they can run out of steam unless all participants really put their backs into keeping them going," he told reporters.

Some politicians fear campaigning for the British election, which must be held by May, will mean the whole Northern Ireland peace process being put on ice for several months unless progress is made very soon.
